extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, ornithologists/herpetologists, and informed general readers interested in sexual selection and animal behaviour
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and observational criteria for identifying, interpreting, and comparing secondary sexual characters (weapons, ornaments, colours, songs, dances, seasonal displays) across reptiles and birds, with emphasis on distinguishing sexual selection from other causes. Emphasises behavioural observation (fighting, display, female choice), seasonal timing, and structural sex-differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sounds (rattle) in mating vs warning
rubrics_metrics.description: The rattle of snakes may serve to "bring the sexes together" (mate attraction) but may also warn predators or even paralyse prey with fear; it is uncertain which sex calls or whether the sound has multiple functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine function by observing whether the sound is associated with pairing (bringing sexes together), which sex calls or remains stationary, and whether alternative uses (warning, startling prey) are evident. Do not assume single function from the existence of the sound alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male fighting (Law of battle) as a driver of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all male birds (and many lizards) are extremely pugnacious, using beaks, wings, legs, and other structures for fighting; such contests can select for larger size and special weapons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe direct male–male combat, frequency during breeding-season, and whether victorious males gain mates. Presence of persistent combative behaviour and weapons (spurs, horns) supports evolution of traits by male rivalry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special weapons as sexual characters (spurs, horns, bony projections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures such as spurs on legs or wings, bony projections or horns on the skull (e.g., in chameleons), and comb‑like appendages are often male-specific and function in fighting or display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sexual dimorphism (present in males, rudimentary or absent in females), variation with season, and observed use in combat or defence of young. Note exceptions where both sexes possess them or where function may be defensive rather than sexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal development and display of ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ornaments (throat pouches, bright colours, crests) are developed or intensified during the pairing-season and are displayed chiefly then.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal onset/intensification of a trait (e.g., throat-pouch colours in Sitana, brighter colours in Calotes maria during breeding) strongly indicates sexual function. Record timing relative to breeding and display behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in colouration (male brightness)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many species males have brighter, more distinctly defined tints and stripes than females; such colours are often attributed to attraction rather than protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare sexes and consider ecological context: if both sexes share bright coloration in concealing habitats the colour may be protective; if males alone (or males more brilliant) and associated with courtship displays, infer sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamental appendages as analogues of other taxa (combs, wattles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendages (e.g., ceratophora snout appendage) may be comparable to combs of gallinaceous birds and apparently serve as ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use morphological analogy and behavioural observation (erection, display) to infer ornamental/sexual role rather than utility for locomotion or feeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male-specific scent organs (pre-anal pores) indicating olfactory courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: Male-only structures such as pre-anal pores in some lizards probably serve to emit an odour for attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note presence/sex-specificity of scent organs and seek evidence of odour-emission linked to courtship or female response before inferring sexual function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioural display patterns (nods, frill erection, tail-waving, dances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Males perform conspicuous gestures and displays (head nods, frill/throat‑pouch erection, tail waving, dances, love-antics) in courtship and rivalry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document specific display actions, their sequence, whether directed at females or rivals, and female reactions. Complex or ritualized displays imply a role in attraction or social signalling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lekking and congregated display sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Some species (e.g., the ruff, capercailzie, black-cock) gather at particular spots where males display and fight while females attend and choose mates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record presence of fixed display arenas, male congregation, female attendance, and mating success of displayed males to evaluate sexual selection via female choice and intrasexual competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female choice vs male victory as determinant of pairing
rubrics_metrics.description: Females may choose males based on display/song rather than automatically accepting victors; battles may be 'sham' displays to show off rather than to injure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess female behaviour (attendance, approach, selection) and post-battle mate choice. Evidence that females prefer certain displays or singers supports female choice as an important mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing sexual selection from natural selection due to ecology
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sexual differences (e.g., beak shape) may result from differences in habits of life (feeding), not sexual selection; e.g., beak variations in humming-birds related to feeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare morphology to ecological roles and behaviour. If a trait aligns with feeding/foraging differences between sexes, consider natural selection; if aligned with courtship/fighting, consider sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of size dimorphism (which sex larger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Males being larger than females often results from advantage in male–male competition; in some species females are larger, possibly for different selective reasons (e.g., female–female competition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure sexual size dimorphism and relate to observed behaviours (fighting, territoriality, parental effort) before attributing cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of display-features as shields or defensive structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Some structures (e.g., the ruff of feathers) may serve as a shield during fighting as well as an ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe how structures are used during combat (defensive posture, shielding) to distinguish protective function from purely ornamental signalling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wing spurs and their sex-differential role
rubrics_metrics.description: Wing spurs occur in some birds; in some species males have larger spurs used in fighting, in others both sexes bear them and use may be chiefly for defence of young.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine relative size between sexes, seasonal change, and observed use (combat vs parental defence) before assigning sexual function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal and instrumental music as sexual signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Bird song and other vocalisations serve multiple functions (distress, alarm, cohesion) but the 'true song' is chiefly uttered in the breeding-season and may charm or call the other sex; singing may also be rivalry/emulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish song types (alarm vs courtship song), document timing (breeding season), female responses, and whether song quality predicts mating success; consider both female choice and male–male competition explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and practice of song as a factor in mate attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Singing is partly an art improved by practice; birds learn songs from foster parents or neighbours and superior singers often gain mates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the best singers obtain mates preferentially (experimental pairing or natural observation) and consider cultural transmission of song in sexual selection analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal mortality and cost of display (song exhaustion, death)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intense singing and display may carry physiological cost (exhaustion, death) and risk, suggesting costly signalling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for display costs when interpreting honesty of sexual signals—extreme investment by males may signal quality to females.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological/physiological correlates of singing (laryngeal muscles)
rubrics_metrics.description: With true songsters the muscles of the larynx may be stronger in males than in females, though vocal organ structure is generally similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine anatomical differences related to vocal performance as supporting evidence for selection on song.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative propensity to sing by body size group
rubrics_metrics.description: Only small birds properly sing; song production is correlated with taxonomic/size groups (Insessores have complex vocal organs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider phylogenetic and biomechanical constraints on song when comparing across taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring function from absence of injury in fights ('sham' battles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where battles rarely produce maimed individuals, contests may be primarily display rather than injurious combat designed to kill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record injury rates and intensity of fights; low injury but high display argues for ritualized competition shaped to advertise rather than to injure.
